::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**A provocative paper, on purpose.** A thesis, a model, a simulation and predictions that could prove it wrong. It follows [Stop Reviewing Pull Requests](../2026-10-23-stop-reviewing-pull-requests/index.qmd), which let go of approving each change. This one lets go of the testing layers around a feature *while it is being built*, and keeps them for when it is done. Figures 1 and 2 are schematics of my own. Figures 3 and 4 and Table 3 come from [sim.py](sim.py) and [figs.py](figs.py). The parameters are chosen, not measured.
:::

**Abstract.** There are two worlds of testing. In the first, we *shift left*: test early, in layers, before anyone uses the software. It gives stability and protects against regressions, at the price of slow learning. In the second, we *ship to learn*: put the feature in front of people who know the domain and correct it every day. It is fast and finds what no test plan foresaw, at the price of fragility. When agents write the code, the defects that survive unit tests are mostly about *fit*: the code does what was asked, but not what the domain needs. Only people who know the domain see those. I propose combining the two worlds in sequence. **Develop** each new feature with unit tests and automatic checks, in production behind a flag, used daily by domain experts. **Lock it in** when it is done, with a regression suite generated from the accepted behaviour, and then flip the flag. A simple model shows that a suite run in every development cycle pays only if $s/T < \ln(1-e\varphi)/\ln(1-q)$. In a simulation, the combined process reaches the market in 7 days instead of 13. It leaves the same number of defects for customers over the first three months, for an eighth of the engineering time. AI does not settle what is right for the domain, and generated tests can lock in mistakes. What we should let go of is not rigour but the belief that a feature can be known to be right before anyone has used it.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Claims

1. **Two worlds.** Shift left gives stability; ship to learn gives fit and speed. Each fails alone. Used in sequence, they keep both strengths.
2. **The rule.** While a feature is built: unit tests, automatic checks, a flag and domain experts every day. When it is done: lock it in with a generated regression suite, then flip the flag.
3. **Why now.** With agents, most remaining defects are about fit. A suite run in every cycle pays only if $s/T < \ln(1-e\varphi)/\ln(1-q)$, and the bound falls as agents improve.
4. **Existing features.** They keep a fully automated regression suite on every build. Nothing here weakens it.
5. **What AI does not solve.** Judging fit, and knowing when a plausible test is wrong. Those stay with people.
6. **What to let go.** Certainty before use, not care. If features built this way escape more defects or cause more regressions, the thesis is wrong.
:::

## 1. Introduction

My thesis: **while a new feature is being developed, the testing layers between the unit test and the user should go.** That means integration and end-to-end suites written as the feature changes, manual test plans, QA passes, staging as a gate and acceptance at the end. They should not shrink. They should wait, until the feature is done.

Every day I see agents write in an hour what used to take a week. What has not sped up is learning whether what was built is right. That knowledge belongs to the people who use the software: application engineers, specialists, experienced internal users. They know what the software is *for*.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**An illustrative case** (made up, but typical). An agent builds a feature that schedules maintenance for equipment. The specification says: next service 90 days after the last one. Unit tests pass, and an end-to-end suite written from the same specification would pass too. On the first afternoon, an application engineer using it notices that the count must restart after a *repair*, not only after a scheduled service, because that is how the equipment is certified. Nobody wrote that down. No test could have caught it, since every test was written from the same specification as the code. The fix ships the next morning.
:::

The usual process shows the feature to that engineer last, after every layer of testing, and each of their findings goes back through every layer (Figure 1, top). The proposal shows it to them first, behind a flag, and keeps the layers for the end (Figure 1, bottom).

## 2. Background

**Shift left.** Early testing rests on the claim that a defect costs one to two orders of magnitude more to fix the later it is found [@boehm1981]. The evidence for that curve is thinner than its fame suggests [@bossavit2015], and agile practice argued that short iterations flatten it [@beck1999]. The practice of moving tests earlier got a name [@smith2001] and a shape, the test pyramid [@cohn2009].

**Ship to learn.** Continuous delivery showed that small, frequent releases are faster and safer [@humble2010; @forsgren2018]. Large web companies separate deploying code from releasing a feature, using flags [@feitelson2013; @savor2016], and flags have known costs [@rahman2016; @hodgson2017]. Using one's own software first is an old habit [@harrison2006]. *Build, measure, learn* treats a release as an experiment [@ries2011], and controlled experiments made that rigorous [@kohavi2020].

**Locking in behaviour.** *Characterization tests* record what a system does, so later changes cannot alter it unnoticed [@feathers2004]. Regression suites are selected and prioritised to run fast on every change [@yoo2012; @memon2017]. Language models now generate useful unit tests [@schafer2024; @alshahwan2024]. Writing tests has become cheap. Knowing which behaviour is right has not.

**The limits of the machine.** Deep learning systems are fluent but brittle outside what they have seen [@marcus2019; @marcus2020]. @quattrociocchi2025 argue that language models reach outputs by a route that differs from human judgement at every stage, from grounding to values. They name *Epistemia* the condition in which plausible output replaces the work of judging it. @capraro2026 warns of the reverse error: coming to see human judgement itself as pattern completion.

## 3. Two worlds

Each world was built for a different problem, and each fails when used alone (Table 1).

| | Shift left | Ship to learn | Together |
|---|---|---|---|
| Built for | code written by hand, costly to change | behaviour that must be discovered in use | features built by agents, cheap to change |
| Finds well | implementation defects, regressions | fit defects, surprises | both, each at its moment |
| Fails at | fit; slow cycles; tests for behaviour that will change | regressions; fragile releases; no lasting safety net | needs experts, a fast fix loop and flag discipline |
| Tests are written | before use, rewritten as the feature moves | rarely | unit tests always; regression suite once, when the feature is done |
| Who judges quality | the test plan | the user | the expert while building, the suite afterwards |

: **Table 1.** Two worlds of testing and their combination.

The combination is not a compromise between them. It uses each world for what it does best, in sequence. While the feature is still changing, the second world rules: learn as fast as possible from people who know the domain, with only the cheap checks that keep the code sane. When the feature stops changing, the first world takes over: lock in the behaviour with a thorough, automated suite, so that it stays correct through every future change. Shift left was right about rigour and wrong about timing. Ship to learn was right about timing and wrong about permanence.

## 4. A model of the development loop

A feature is built in cycles of length $T$, here one working day. *Implementation defects* mean the code does not do what was specified; a machine can detect them. *Fit defects* mean the code does what was specified, but not what the domain needs. Let $\varphi$ be the share of implementation defects among those left. Experts using the feature in place find a share $q$ of the remaining defects each cycle. A suite run in every cycle adds $s$ to it and catches a share $e$ of implementation defects. It catches almost no fit defects, because it is written from the same specification as the code. Without the suite, remaining defects are multiplied by $(1-q)$ every $T$. With it, they are multiplied by roughly $(1-q)(1-e\varphi)$ every $T+s$. The suite speeds up learning when

$$
\frac{\ln(1-q) + \ln(1-e\varphi)}{T + s} < \frac{\ln(1-q)}{T}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{s}{T} < \frac{\ln(1-e\varphi)}{\ln(1-q)} .
$$ {#eq-suite}

*The suite must cost a smaller share of the cycle than the share of learning it adds.* Take $e = 0.6$, half the defects of each kind, and experts who find half of what remains each day. The bound is then about $0.51$: under four hours in an eight-hour cycle.

**What agents change.** First, $T$ shrinks, so a fixed $s$ becomes a large part of each cycle. Second, $\varphi$ falls: agents with unit tests increasingly do what they are told, so most remaining mistakes are in what they were told. As $\varphi \to 0$, the bound goes to zero. *Assumption F: for features built by agents with unit tests, most defects that survive the unit tests are fit defects.* Prediction H3 tests it.

**Why $s$ is large while a feature moves.** A suite's cost is not its run time. It is writing tests for behaviour that changes every day, rewriting them, rerunning the flaky ones [@luo2014], and deciding for each failure whether the code or the test is wrong. Once the feature is accepted, its behaviour stops moving, and the same tests are written once and stay valid (Figure 2).

## 5. The rule in practice

**Developing a new feature.** Before production, only checks that run in minutes: the build, types and linters, static analysis, dependency and security scans, and unit tests for each changed behaviour. No test may be deleted or weakened without a recorded decision. The feature then goes to production behind a flag. Three to five domain experts use it in their real work, an hour or two a day, and note what they find. Where possible, the agent turns each finding into a unit test.

**Done: lock it in.** When the experts go two days without a new finding, the feature is done, and its behaviour is stable enough to test in depth. The agent generates the regression suite from the accepted behaviour. It contains characterization tests taken from the experts' sessions, end-to-end scenarios for the main paths, and unit tests for every edge case the experts found. A person, ideally one of the experts, reads the suite's scenarios and confirms that they describe what should happen. The suite is then automated on every build, and the flag is flipped in stages [@beyer2016; @kohavi2020]. Where the domain requires formal quality control, it happens here, once, on the build that will be released.

**Existing features.** Everything already in the market keeps its automated regression suite on every build, and a failure blocks the build. A new feature changes shared code, and that is where regressions come from. This suite is what lets the expert loop move fast without breaking what customers rely on.

**Always.** Every build is rolled out in stages with automatic rollback. The thin gate of the previous paper still applies to what cannot be undone, because a flag does not make a deleted table reversible. Once a feature is released, its flag and the old code path are removed [@rahman2016].

## 6. A simulation

I simulated one feature under five policies, then the 60 working days after its release, during which changes elsewhere break it from time to time (Table 2). The suite run in every cycle costs one working day. Lock-in is the same suite, run once after acceptance and kept on every build afterwards. The parameters are chosen, not measured, and generous to the suite.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Defects in the first version | 12, $\varphi = 0.5$ |
| Cycle without suite, $T$ | 1 working day |
| Suite per cycle, $s$ | 1 day, 4 engineer hours (2 h in Figure 3) |
| Lock-in | the same suite once: 1 day, 4 engineer hours |
| Unit tests catch | 50% of new implementation defects and of regressions |
| Suite catches, $e$ | 60% of implementation, 10% of fit defects, 70% of regressions |
| Experts find per day | 60% of implementation, 40% of fit defects |
| Chance a fix adds a defect | 15% |
| After release | 60 working days; a regression arrives on 5% of days |
| Done when | 2 days in a row with nothing found (1 to 5 in Figure 3) |
| Runs | 4 000 per policy |

: **Table 2.** Simulation parameters. *Shift left* runs the suite until it finds nothing, then hands over to experts. The other policies test in place from day one.

| Policy | Days to market (p90) | Escaped at release | Regressions, 60 days | Suite hours |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shift left | 13.2 (17.8) | 0.39 | 0.46 | 30 |
| Suite + flag | 12.0 (16.0) | 0.33 | 0.46 | 24 |
| Unit tests + flag | 6.0 (9.0) | 0.47 | 1.48 | 0 |
| **Two worlds: flag, then lock-in** | **7.0 (9.1)** | **0.39** | **0.46** | **4** |
| No tests + flag | 7.0 (9.0) | 0.46 | 2.99 | 0 |

: **Table 3.** Results for one feature: median days to market (90th percentile), defects left for customers at release, regressions that reach customers in the next 60 working days, and engineer hours on the suite. Standard errors are 0.01 or less. Run `python sim.py` to reproduce them.

**Together, the two worlds reach the market in half the time with the same quality.** The combined process releases in 7 days instead of 13.2. It leaves the same number of defects for customers at release (0.39) and over the following three months (0.46), for 4 engineer hours on the suite instead of 30.

**The second world alone is fast but fragile.** With unit tests and a flag only, the feature ships a day sooner. It then lets three times as many regressions through, 1.48 instead of 0.46, because nothing protects it once the experts move on. The lock-in does not find many new bugs in the feature: one more day of expert use would remove about as many (Figure 3). Its value is that it keeps the feature working afterwards.

**The first world alone is safe but slow.** Running the suite in every cycle removes a few more defects before release (0.33). But each cycle takes twice as long, and the same gain comes sooner from more days of expert use (Figure 3, top). When the suite costs two hours instead of a day, the policies almost meet (Figure 3, bottom), as @eq-suite predicts: for these values the bound lies between three and six hours (Figure 4).

## 7. What AI will not solve

This proposal depends on agents being fast, but it does not ask them to judge, and it should not.

**Fit is not in the specification.** An agent can only build from what it is told. The maintenance rule in section 1 was in no document, only in the engineer's experience of how the equipment is certified. Language models lack that grounding in a world they have not experienced [@quattrociocchi2025], and they are brittle beyond what they have seen [@marcus2020]. That is why the expert, not the agent, decides when a feature is done.

**Generated tests can lock in mistakes.** A characterization test records what the system does, not what it should do [@feathers2004]. If a fit defect survives the loop, the lock-in will faithfully protect it. A generated suite that passes produces exactly the feeling of knowing without judgement that @quattrociocchi2025 call Epistemia. So a person who knows the domain reads the scenarios before they become the reference, and treats a green suite as evidence, not proof.

**Experts are not language models.** It would be easy to conclude that if agents write code and tests, they could soon replace the experts too. @capraro2026 describes the bias behind that conclusion: seeing human judgement as one more form of pattern completion. The expert's value lies in what the model lacks: knowing what matters here, noticing what is missing, and being able to say "I don't know yet, let me use it tomorrow".

**Accountability does not move.** When a feature is released, someone answers for it. Agents make building and fixing cheap; they do not make responsibility cheap.

## 8. Predictions and a test protocol

For features built with the two worlds in sequence, compared with similar features built with the full suite in every cycle:

- **H1. Faster to market.** Median time from first commit to the flag being flipped for everyone falls by at least a third.
- **H2. No more escaped defects.** Customer-reported defects in the 30 days after the flip are no more frequent, within a margin fixed in advance.
- **H3. Most remaining defects are about fit (Assumption F).** Fewer than half of what experts find in place could have been caught by an integration or end-to-end test, as judged by someone outside the team.
- **H4. No more regressions.** The change failure rate of code outside the flag [@forsgren2018] does not rise, and locked-in features break no more often in the following six months.
- **H5. The experts stay engaged.** Participation and findings per expert hour do not decay over the study.

**Protocol.** Within the same teams, features are randomly assigned to one process at the start. H2 and H4 are pre-registered non-inferiority tests. H1, H3 and H5 are secondary, measured from the repository, the flag system, the defect tracker and incident logs. If H2 or H4 fails, the thesis is wrong for those teams. If H3 fails, its reasoning is wrong, even if the outcome looks good.

## 9. Objections and limitations

**"Testing in production is reckless."** Without a flag, staged rollout and rollback, it is. Here customers cannot reach the code. The real risk is the flag itself. In 2012, a trading firm reused an old flag that woke up dead code on the one server of eight that had not been updated, and it lost about 460 million dollars in 45 minutes [@sec2013knight]. Flags are code. Each needs a unit test showing that, when off, the old behaviour is untouched, plus an owner and a removal date.

**"Experts are not testers."** They are not meant to be. Testers know how to break software; experts know what it is for. Their time is scarce, and if the loop becomes an extra duty, $q$ falls and the advantage with it. The loop works when using the new version is part of their real work.

**"Production data is real."** Flagged features may write only what could be corrected by hand. Anything that cannot be undone goes through the thin gate. Where privacy or regulation forbids it, the loop runs on a copy of production.

**"Intent Is the Source said tests are the source."** [It did](../2026-10-21-intent-is-the-source/index.qmd), and the two papers agree. While a feature moves, unit tests state its intent. Once it is accepted, the regression suite states it for good.

**Limits of the model.** It treats defects as independent and equally severe. It assumes $q$ is constant, although experts may find obvious problems first. The regression rate and the suite's catch rate after release are assumed, not measured. The direction of the result holds wherever @eq-suite holds, not its size. And it assumes agents make writing and fixing fast, which the evidence for experienced developers does not yet settle [@becker2025].

## 10. Conclusion: what to let go

It would be easy to read this paper as "AI is fast, so test less". That is not the claim. The proposal keeps every automated check, writes a full regression suite for every feature and protects everything already in the market. It asks more of the people who know the domain, not less.

What it lets go of is one belief: that we can know a feature is right before anyone has used it. Shift left was built on that belief, and with code written by hand it was a reasonable bet. Layers of tests written from a specification gave a feeling of certainty, but they could only confirm what the specification already said. The most important question, whether we built the right thing, was answered last, when it was most expensive to change.

Letting go of that certainty is not letting go of care. It means testing at the moment the tests mean something: learning from use while the feature still moves, locking it in once it has stopped. Machines run the checks. People judge the fit. Build with the people who know, then make it last.
